author: David Swanson
title: Between Disaster and Foreign Interference: Lessons in Peace and Solidarity in the Wake of the Earthquake in Venezuela
content:
By IPB Council Member and WBW Latin America Organizer Gabriel Aguirre, August 9, 2026

Imagine returning home after a holiday and realizing you’ve lost everything: family, friends, acquaintances, your home, everything you once thought would be forever. This was the reality many Venezuelans faced after the double earthquake that struck the country on June 24th. According to experts, these seismic events measured 7.1 and 7.3 on the Richter scale, occurring just 39 seconds apart.

It’s impossible to describe the catastrophic consequences of this natural event. The last major earthquake in Venezuela was in 1967. Almost 60 years later, a more intense earthquake with more dramatic consequences struck. The earthquake primarily impacted three central states located in the northern coastal region of the country: La Guaira, Caracas, and Miranda. Other states were also affected, but to a lesser extent.

At the time of writing this report, more than 6,000 people have died, many are missing, and nearly 6,000 have been rescued from the rubble. Undoubtedly, in the aftermath of the earthquake in Venezuela, we must acknowledge the solidarity of the world, which immediately sent rescuers and humanitarian aid to the country. This, along with the actions of rescue teams, firefighters, and the country’s security forces, allowed for the rescue and care of a significant number of people.

title: Mayor of Hiroshima Delivers Peace Declaration
content:
By City of Hiroshima, August 9, 2026

The City of Hiroshima PEACE DECLARATION August 6, 2026

Even now, 81 years after the atomic bombings, right here on Earth where we live, we still see military invasions using nuclear weapons as tools of intimidation as well as other imperious actions by major powers in violation of international law. This year’s Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) Review Conference failed for the third consecutive time to adopt a final document. The responsibility for this failure lies with political leaders who place blame on others to justify their own behavior. The words and actions of such leaders shake the foundations of global peace and stability while ignoring the obligations set forth by the NPT.

If this continues, mistrust will deepen around the world, driving us back toward the rampant greed of the World War II era. Downplaying the inhumanity of nuclear weapons and accepting the use of force to pursue one’s own prosperity risk cycles of violent retaliation that could ultimately result in another Hiroshima or Nagasaki.

title: Canadians: 1. Elbit: 0. — Our First #ElbitOut Victory
content:

Less than a month after launching the #ElbitOutOfCanada campaign, we have already secured our first victory.

“There are no current orders for Elbit, and none will be accepted going forward,” the Chief Operating Officer wrote to the Arms Embargo Now Team.

And Apollo is not the only company we’ve heard from. It’s clear that our efforts to take an arms embargo into our own hands are working. Companies all across the country are paying attention— and some of them are already signalling a willingness to cut ties with Elbit to avoid public scrutiny.

But we’re just getting started. On August 13th, we’re putting local Elbit suppliers on notice from coast to coast to coast.

Together, we’re sending them a clear message: drop your ties with Elbit Systems or face the reputational and financial consequences of your ongoing complicity in Israel’s genocide.

title: Volunteer Spotlight: Baltimore Chapter Co-Coordinator Ronda Cooperstein
content:
Each month, we share the stories of World BEYOND War volunteers around the world. Want to volunteer with World BEYOND War? Email greta@worldbeyondwar.org.

I became an anti-war activist at a young age, after reading many books about Indigenous peoples across the globe. I was shocked and appalled at the violence inflicted on so many innocent populations in the name of civilization. Once in college, in the late 70’s, I became active on campus, joining and supporting groups that worked for peace and justice. As a Jewish American, I became very active in issues related to Israel/Palestine and went on to found a local organization, Baltimore Jews for Israeli Palestinian Peace. After years and years of working locally on these issues, I decided to start a chapter of World BEYOND War in Baltimore. I was inspired by the Ukrainian conscientious objector, Yurii Sheliazhenko, who is a Board Member of World BEYOND War.

Our local chapter, since forming a little over a year ago, has worked mainly on issues related to Israel/Palestine, hosting Combatants for Peace, bringing Israeli genocide scholar Omer Bartov to Baltimore, and holding vigils. We also lobby our Congress members to support all anti-war legislation and to take a stand against militarism at all levels. Last summer we co-sponsored the local Hiroshima/Nagasaki Memorial event. This was a criminal action based on lies that killed over a million people, injured over 4 million people, made homeless over 4 million people, left behind permanent environmental devastation, shattered the rule of law, generated terrorism, impeded global collaboration on non-optional crises, diverted trillions of dollars away from desperate needs, shredded our civil liberties, fueled bigotry and xenophobia, militarized policing, and led in a fairly straight line to the catastrophe we’re in right now.

title: War Is So Inevitable That Governments Have to Spend Our Money to Lie to Our Kids to Recruit Them or We’d Have No Wars
content:
THE SQUARE | RAF Recruitment and Peace Protest in Luton | Short Observational Documentary

By Zakir Hossain, August 4, 2026

THE SQUARE is a short observational documentary filmed during an RAF public engagement event in George Square, Luton. As families explore aircraft exhibits and recruitment activities, a small group of peace campaigners quietly distribute anti-war leaflets around the square. The film observes two contrasting perspectives sharing the same public space. Through conversations with RAF personnel, peace activists and the unfolding events themselves, THE SQUARE invites viewers to reflect on recruitment, protest, remembrance and the different ways people understand war. Location: George Square, Luton, United Kingdom.

It’s an honour to be here on unceded sovereign Gadigal land and I want to begin by acknowledging that this always was and always will be Aboriginal land.

Eighty one years ago this month, a uranium bomb was detonated by the United States over the city Hiroshima, on August 6, 1945. It flattened and burned around 70% of the city and, by the end of that year, at least 140,000 people had died.

Three days later a larger plutonium bomb exploded over Nagasaki, killing 74,000 people by the end of that year. Ground temperatures in Nagasaki reached 4000°C and radioactive rain poured down.

The survivors of the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, known as the Hibakush a, lived with massively increased rates of cancer and chronic diseases, some being passed to the next generations.

As a doctor and neurosurgeon, I am often called upon to treat severely injured people and, apart from the fact that this awful poisonous incineration was entirely preventable, I find it unspeakable that in Hiroshima and Nagasaki, no meaningful humanitarian response was possible.

title: The Wars Are Still Based on Lies
content:

By David Swanson, World BEYOND War, July 28, 2026

Excerpted from War Is Still A Lie .

Since I wrote War Is A Lie in 2010 and updated it in 2015, the lies used to prop up wars have varied but continued. My summary remains true:

Not a single thing that we commonly believe about wars that helps keep them around is true. Wars cannot be good or glorious. Nor can they be justified as a means of achieving peace or anything else of value. The reasons given for wars, before, during, and after them (often three very different sets of reasons for the same war) are all false. It is common to imagine that, because we’d never go to war without a good reason, having gone to war, we simply must have a good reason. This needs to be reversed. Because there can be no good reason for war, having gone to war, we are participating in a lie.

But some things have changed. The Iraq Syndrome has ended. title: World BEYOND War Supports WILPF’s 34th International Congress in Cameroon
content:
By Guy Feugap, Africa Organizer of World BEYOND War




For four days from 17 to 20 July 2026, Cameroon hosted the 34th international congress of the Women’s International League for Peace and Freedom (WILPF). Organized by the WILPF Cameroon section in a hybrid format, the congress, WILPF’s highest decision-making body, marked an important milestone for both Cameroon and the global feminist peace movement. Delegates from more than forty national sections elected a new International Board, re-elected Cameroonian peace leader Sylvie Jacqueline Ndongmo as International President, and committed again to advancing feminist peace in a world increasingly affected by war, militarization and injustice. World BEYOND War supported WILPF Cameroon in organizing this event.




Hosting the Congress in Cameroon carried a symbolic significance. Although often perceived as a relatively stable country in Africa, Cameroon has been deeply affected by multiple and overlapping crises. Armed conflict in the North-West and South-West regions, violent extremism in the Far North, the arrival of refugees from neighboring countries, and intercommunal and political tensions have all placed immense pressure on communities, with women and children bearing a disproportionate share of the consequences. title: Cross-Country Peace March Passes Through Osaka, Japan
content:
By Gerry Yokota, Co-Coordinator of the World BEYOND War Japan Chapter, World BEYOND War, July 14, 2026

The annual Cross-Country Peace March—a relay march transversing all 47 Japanese prefectures over several months—began in May and will culminate in Hiroshima in early August, ahead of the 2026 World Conference against Atomic and Hydrogen Bombs.

Marchers are walking thousands of kilometers from Hokkaido in the north to Okinawa in the south along designated national highways. Local municipal networks organize daily handovers of peace banners and petitions containing thousands of signatures urging the Japanese government to sign and ratify the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW) before the Review Conference scheduled for November 2026.

The provisional program for this year’s World Conference against A and Hydrogen Bombs indicates a focus on four major areas: (1) the systematic dismantling of traditional nuclear deterrence theory in international relations; (2) civil society solidarity; (3) hibakusha testimony, including that of Korean hibakusha and communities impacted by nuclear testing in the Marshall Islands; and (4) youth diplomacy, focusing on intergenerational knowledge transfer.
